title: Board discovery's `[ -c /dev/$tty ]` check is always true: containers without the cgroup rule (the demo included) add host boards they cannot open, and the new hint never prints
description: This is the earlier finding 'Board discovery reads the host's sysfs but never checks the container's /dev', and its fix is done wrongly. The fix rests on the comment at lines 77-79: 'The node is made only where the device cgroup allows it (mknod needs the same permission as open), so its absence is the answer.' That premise is false. runc always appends 'c *:* m' and 'b *:* m' to every container's device rules, and Docker grants CAP_MKNOD by default. So sync_devices (line 55) creates /dev/ttyACMn for every host tty in every container, with or without compose's device_cgroup_rules. find_boards then sees a character device, echoes the tty, and never reaches the 'may not use it ... --device-cgroup-rule' hint at lines 83-84. The other half of the earlier fix, skipping auto-discovery when ESP32C5_DEMO is set, is missing: run_kismet still calls sources() at line 178 after starting the fake board.
failure_scenario: (1) On the Pi with its four boards, run `docker compose --profile demo up demo`; the demo service has no device_cgroup_rules. The fake board starts, then sync_devices creates /dev/ttyACM0-3 and find_boards returns all four. Kismet gets sources esp32c5-ttyACM0..3:mode=wifi next to the demo source, and each keeps failing with 'cannot open /dev/ttyACM0: Operation not permitted'. (2) `docker run --cap-add NET_ADMIN -p 2501:2501 esp32c5-kismet` on a Linux host with a board, without --device-cgroup-rule: the log shows 'source: esp32c5-ttyACM0:mode=wifi' and never the hint that names the missing rule. (3) Each container the smoke test starts on the Pi adds the Pi's boards as failing sources. The checks still pass, because running= counts only running sources.
evidence:
entrypoint.sh:55 `mknod -m 660 "$node" c "$major" "$minor" 2>/dev/null || true`; :77-80 the comment quoted above, then `if [ -c "/dev/$tty" ]; then echo "$tty"`; :166-178 the demo block, then `defs=$(sources)` unconditionally.
Experiments on Docker Desktop 29.8, throwaway --rm containers:
(a) `docker run --rm debian:trixie-slim sh -c 'mknod -m 660 /dev/ttyACM7 c 166 7 && ...; [ -c /dev/ttyACM7 ]; exec 3<>/dev/ttyACM7'` printed `mknod ok: crw-rw---- 1 root root 166, 7`, `test -c true`, `cannot create /dev/ttyACM7: Operation not permitted`. With --device-cgroup-rule 'c 166:* rmw' the open got past the cgroup (ENXIO, no such device).
(b) The repo's own entrypoint.sh lines 27-100, sourced in a container with a fake /sys/class/tty/ttyACM0 (dev 166:0, USB 303a:1001) and no rule, printed `find_boards -> [ttyACM0]`, `sources -> [ esp32c5-ttyACM0:mode=wifi]` and `open: ... /dev/ttyACM0: Operation not permitted`. No hint was printed.
(c) dash 0.5.12's `[ -r n ] && [ -w n ]` goes through faccessat2, which applies the device cgroup without opening the device. No rule: false for ttyACM0 and ttyACM7. With 'c 166:* rmw': true for both. With 'c 166:7 rmw': ttyACM0 false, ttyACM7 true.
suggested_fix: At line 80, test access as well as existence: `if [ -c "/dev/$tty" ] && [ -r "/dev/$tty" ] && [ -w "/dev/$tty" ]; then`. The device cgroup applies to access(2), which dash's test uses, so this answers per node, handles a single --device /dev/ttyACM0 correctly, and never opens the port, so DTR and RTS are not touched. On a system without faccessat2 it falls back to today's behaviour. Correct the comment at 77-79. In run_kismet, skip auto-discovery when the demo board is running and no sources are listed: `defs=""; if [ "$n" -eq 0 ] || [ -n "${KISMET_SOURCES:-}" ]; then defs=$(sources); fi`.

On a system without faccessat2 it falls back to today's behaviour. Correct the comment at 77-79. verdicts:
The finding holds. I checked it against the current files and ran throwaway containers on Docker Desktop 29.8, named vfy-* and removed with --rm; the scratch files are deleted too.

1. **The comment's premise is false.** Lines 77-79 of docker/entrypoint.sh say "mknod needs the same permission as open". It does not: mknod needs the device cgroup's 'm' access, open needs 'r' and 'w'. runc adds 'c *:* m' and 'b *:* m' to every container, and Docker grants CAP_MKNOD by default.
   - With no rule in debian:trixie-slim, `mknod /dev/ttyACM7 c 166 7` succeeded, `[ -c ]` was true, and opening the node failed with "Operation not permitted".
   - With `--device-cgroup-rule 'c 166:* rmw'`, the open got past the cgroup and failed with ENXIO (no such device).
   - With `--cap-drop MKNOD`, mknod itself failed. So only CAP_MKNOD and 'm' decide whether the node gets made.

2. **Nothing guards the path.** sync_devices (line 55) runs mknod for every host ttyACM/ttyUSB it sees in sysfs, and the `|| true` hides nothing, because mknod succeeds. find_boards (line 80) checks only `[ -c ]`, so it echoes every host board. The hint at lines 83-84 is unreachable whenever CAP_MKNOD is present.

title: The 'anything else' role never creates the device nodes, so a capture helper run through the image cannot open a board it lists
description: Side effect of replacing the /dev bind with device nodes the container makes itself. Only run_kismet (line 164) and run_helper (line 229) call keep_devices_in_sync. The third role, `*) exec "$@"`, runs the command in Docker's own /dev, which has no ttyACM or ttyUSB nodes. The header (line 8) offers this role for commands such as `kismet_cap_esp32c5 --list` or `sh`. --list still works, because the C helper's list_callback reads only sysfs. But any capture started from that role fails, even in a container that has the 166/188 cgroup rules and NET_ADMIN. With the old /dev bind it worked.
failure_scenario: To debug a board on the Pi, run `docker compose run --rm helper sh`. That container has device_cgroup_rules and NET_ADMIN, but gets the exec role because of the command override. Inside it, `kismet_cap_esp32c5 --list` shows esp32c5-ttyACM0. `kismet_cap_esp32c5 --connect kismet-host:2501 --source esp32c5-ttyACM0` then fails with 'cannot open /dev/ttyACM0: No such file or directory' and retries forever. The same happens with `docker run --rm --device-cgroup-rule 'c 166:* rmw' --cap-add NET_ADMIN esp32c5-kismet kismet_cap_esp32c5 --connect host:2501 --source esp32c5-ttyACM0`.
evidence: entrypoint.sh:8 `anything else   run as a command, e.g. "kismet_cap_esp32c5 --list" or "sh".`; :255-265 `case "${1:-kismet}" in kismet) ... run_kismet ... helper) run_helper ... *) exec "$@" ;;`. keep_devices_in_sync is called only at :164 and :229. capture_esp32c5.c: list_callback uses find_boards()/tty_is_board(), which read only sysfs. resolve_device returns "/dev/<tty>" for tty* names as they are. serial_open reports `cannot open %s: %s`. In the throwaway containers above, `mknod /dev/ttyACM7` succeeded where the node would otherwise be, confirming that Docker's /dev holds no ttyACM nodes by default.
suggested_fix: Make the nodes once before running the command: `*) sync_devices; exec "$@" ;;`. Use a single pass rather than keep_devices_in_sync, so that a `docker exec ... esp32c5-kismet sh` does not leave a background resync loop behind in the running container. Optionally, say in the header that boards replugged later appear only in the kismet and helper roles.
fix:
In docker/entrypoint.sh, change the last branch to:

    *)
        keep_devices_in_sync
        exec "$@"
        ;;

This matches run_kismet and run_helper. The loop does not outlive the container, because it ends when the exec'd PID 1 exits. `docker exec` does not run the entrypoint, so the fix leaves no loop behind in an already running container. A helper started from this role can then follow a board that comes back as another ttyACM number after a mode-switch reboot or replug.

If only one pass is wanted, `sync_devices; exec "$@"` is enough for `--list` and a first open, but not for that re-enumeration case. Either way, update the header comment at line 8 to say this role also makes the board nodes.
verdicts:
I traced the finding through the current files and it holds. One detail of the suggested fix is based on a wrong premise.

How the failure happens:
- In docker/entrypoint.sh, only run_kismet (line 164) and run_helper (line 229) call keep_devices_in_sync. The same is true of sync_devices, which run_kismet also calls in its wait loop at line 186.
- The `*) exec "$@"` branch at line 264 runs the command without making any device nodes. The Dockerfile sets ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/esp32c5-kismet"], so `docker compose run --rm helper sh` or `docker run IMAGE kismet_cap_esp32c5 ...` goes to that branch. Compose keeps the helper service's device_cgroup_rules and cap_add when the command is overridden, so the container is allowed to use the boards but has no nodes for them.
- In capture_esp32c5.c, list_callback gets its boards from find_boards() and tty_is_board(), which read only /sys/class/tty. So `--list` shows esp32c5-ttyACM0.
- resolve_device (lines 420-425) returns "/dev/ttyACM0" for a tty* name without checking that the node exists. serial_open (lines 550-551) then fails with "cannot open /dev/ttyACM0: No such file or directory". That call is reached from open_callback at line 1410.

Experiment: a throwaway container (`docker run --rm --name vfy-exec-role-devnodes --device-cgroup-rule 'c 166:* rmw' --cap-add NET_ADMIN debian:trixie-slim`) showed a /dev with only core, fd, full, mqueue, null, ptmx, pts, random, shm, stdin/stdout/stderr, tty, urandom and zero. There was no tt

title: The port lock no longer works between the container and the host, or between two containers: each container's /dev/ttyACMn is its own inode, and flock locks an inode
description: Today's C helper, and the Python helper through pyserial's exclusive=True, keep one process per board with flock(LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB) on the device node (capture_esp32c5.c:549-567). flock conflicts only between opens of the same inode. sync_devices now runs mknod for every port in the container's private /dev tmpfs. So the container's /dev/ttyACM0 is a different inode from the host's devtmpfs /dev/ttyACM0 and from the /dev/ttyACM0 of any other container, even though all of them are the same tty. Before the change, the host's /dev was bound in, the inode was shared, and a second user of a board got "already in use". Now a lock taken in one place is invisible everywhere else. Inside a single container the lock still works, because every helper there opens the same node.
failure_scenario: On the Pi, `sudo docker compose up -d` starts the kismet service with restart: unless-stopped, and it comes back at every boot with a source on every board. The user then runs the host-side hardware tests (native kismet_cap_esp32c5, the Python helper, or a native Kismet) on /dev/ttyACM0. Their flock on the host inode succeeds while the container's helper holds its own lock on the container inode. Both helpers send MODE/CHANNELS/START to the same board. A MODE for another radio reboots the board under the other helper, and both read one interleaved byte stream. The tests fail with lost-sync / "no capture for 15 seconds" errors that look like firmware or helper bugs, not with "already in use". The same happens with `docker compose --profile helper up -d` without a service name (compose.yaml:18 says this starts both services): the kismet and helper containers both auto-discover and open every board, and neither is refused.
evidence: Experiment (Docker Desktop 29.8, debian:trixie-slim): two nodes of one device, `mknod /tmp/host-node c 1 3; mknod /tmp/container-node c 1 3`, different inodes (825207 and 825208). With `flock -n -x /tmp/host-node sleep 3` running: a second lock on host-node gives "same node: second lock refused (as intended)", and a lock on container-node gives "other node, same device 1:3: second lock TAKEN -- no exclusion". entrypoint.sh:55 `mknod -m 660 "$node" c "$major" "$minor"`. capture_esp32c5.c:555-560: "...It sits on the device node, so it covers the /dev/serial/by-id links as well... if (flock(fd, LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB) < 0)".
suggested_fix: This is for the C helper run, not this file. After the flock, also set `ioctl(fd, TIOCEXCL)`. TIOCEXCL lives on the tty itself, not on the inode, so it holds across containers and the host for any opener without CAP_SYS_ADMIN. That covers container helpers and any helper after cf_drop_most_caps, which runs before open_callback. Treat EBUSY from open() as PORT_BUSY. Until then, say in compose.yaml and the entrypoint header that the lock does not cross the container boundary: stop the kismet service before using the same boards from the host or from the helper service.
fix:
Keep the flock, and also set TTY_EXCLUSIVE on the tty itself. That flag lives on the tty_struct, not on a node's inode, so it holds between the host and containers, and between two containers.

1. **C helper, serial_open.** Right after the flock succeeds, call `ioctl(fd, TIOCEXCL)`. When open() fails with errno EBUSY, return PORT_BUSY with the same "already in use by another capture" message (errno can be read before snprintf). drop_port already closes before reopen_port, so the helper never refuses itself.

2. **Python helper, esp32c5_kismet/board.py open_serial.** It needs the same step, because pyserial's `exclusive=True` is only flock. After `ser.open()`, call `fcntl.ioctl(ser.fd, termios.TIOCEXCL)` on POSIX. Make port_busy_error treat errno 16 (EBUSY) from the open as IN_USE.

3. **Remaining limit, to document.** TIOCEXCL does not stop an opener that still has CAP_SYS_ADMIN, for example a Python helper or esptool run with sudo, or a setuid-root kismet_cap started by a non-root user (cf_drop_most_caps only drops when getuid()==0).

4. **Until the helpers change.** In compose.yaml and the entrypoint's Serial devices comment, say that the port lock does not cross the container boundary. Tell users to stop the kismet service (`docker compose stop kismet`) before using the same boards from the host or from the helper service, and to always name the service with `--profile helper up -d helper`.
verdicts:
I could not refute it. The mechanism holds in the current files and in a live test.

1. **The inodes differ.** sync_devices (entrypoint.sh:42-62) creates every ttyACM/ttyUSB node itself, with `mknod -m 660 "$node" c "$major" "$minor"` at line 55, inside the container's own /dev tmpfs. compose.yaml no longer binds the host's /dev. The earlier findings file (docker-findings-before.txt, entry 9) shows the old compose had `- /dev:/dev`, and that shared the host devtmpfs inode.

2. **The helper's lock is only flock.** serial_open in capture_esp32c5.c:546-570 does `flock(fd, LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB)` and nothing else. The comment there even says it was chosen instead of TIOCEXCL. The Python helper uses pyserial's `exclusive=True` (board.py:394), which is also flock only. flock state lives on the inode of the node that was opened, not on the tty.

3. **Experiment.** Two throwaway debian:trixie-slim containers on Docker Desktop 29.8 each ran `mknod /dev/lockprobe c 1 3`. The nodes were on different filesystems (st_dev 145 and 153).
   - Container A held `flock -n -x`.
   - Container B took its own lock at the same time: "lock TAKEN while A holds its node".
   - Control: a second lock on the same node inside B was refused, and A's own second lock was refused.
   - Host devtmpfs versus a container tmpfs is the same case: a different superblock, so a different inode.

4. **Reachable.**
   - The kismet service has `restart: unless-stopped`, finds every 303a:1001 board, and Kismet starts a local

title: Wrong assumption: under Docker, mknod works for every device whatever the cgroup allows, so boards the container may not open are still used as sources, and the hint never prints
description: find_boards decides whether the container may use a board by whether sync_devices managed to make its node. The comment says "The node is made only where the device cgroup allows it (mknod needs the same permission as open)". That is false with Docker's defaults. runc always adds `c *:* m` and `b *:* m` (mknod for any device), and CAP_MKNOD is a default capability. The device cgroup only refuses the later open() (EPERM). So on any Linux host, every 303a:1001 tty gets a node and becomes a source, whether or not the container has `c 166:* rmw`. The else branch with the fix-it hint (lines 83-84) can only run under rootless Docker or userns-remap. This was the earlier finding that the demo picks up boards it cannot open, and it is back.
failure_scenario: (1) On the Pi or the Linux PC with boards plugged in, `docker compose --profile demo up demo` runs a service with no device_cgroup_rules. Next to the fake board, Kismet gets esp32c5-ttyACM0..3:mode=wifi. Every one fails with "cannot open /dev/ttyACM0: Operation not permitted" and Kismet retries them, filling its messages. (2) `docker run --cap-add NET_ADMIN -p 2501:2501 esp32c5-kismet`, following the Dockerfile header (lines 17-19, which leave out the cgroup rule), adds every board and every source fails with EPERM. The hint that would name the missing `--device-cgroup-rule 'c 166:* rmw'` never appears.
evidence: Experiment, with no rule: `mknod -m 660 /dev/ttyACM0 c 166 0` gives "mknod 166:0 succeeded" (also block 8:9 and char 4:73 succeed), and opening it gives "cannot create /dev/ttyACM0: Operation not permitted". With `--device-cgroup-rule 'c 166:* rmw'`: mknod succeeds and open gives "No such device or address" (allowed; there is no device in Docker Desktop). entrypoint.sh:77-80 "The node is made only where the device cgroup allows it (mknod needs the same permission as open), so its absence is the answer... if [ -c \"/dev/$tty\" ]; then echo \"$tty\"".
suggested_fix: Test the cgroup on a minor that no board uses, since opening the real port would move DTR/RTS. Once per major, run `mknod /dev/.probe-166 c 166 255` and open it with `( exec 3<>/dev/.probe-166 ) 2>&1`. EPERM means the container may not use that major. ENODEV/ENXIO means it may (there is simply no device there). Remove the probe node afterwards. Use that result, not `[ -c ]`, to choose between listing the board and printing the hint. Correct the comment, and add `--device-cgroup-rule 'c 166:* rmw'` to the docker run example in the Dockerfile header.
fix:
In docker/entrypoint.sh:

1. **Remember the pre-existing nodes.** At the start of `keep_devices_in_sync`, before the first `sync_devices`, save the list of /dev/ttyACM* and /dev/ttyUSB* nodes that already exist. Docker put those there with `--device` or a bind mount, so the container may use them whatever the probe says.

2. **Probe each major once.** Replace the `[ -c ]` test in `find_boards` with a probe that runs once per major (166, 188), for example `may_use_major()`:
   - `p=/dev/.esp32c5-probe-$major`
   - `rm -f "$p"; mknod -m 600 "$p" c "$major" 255 2>/dev/null || return 1`
   - `msg=$( ( exec 3<>"$p" ) 2>&1 ); rm -f "$p"`
   - `case $msg in *'not permitted'*) return 1 ;; esac; return 0`

   ENXIO or ENODEV means the major is allowed and minor 255 is simply unused. The probe never opens a real board, so DTR and RTS do not move. Cache the result per major.

3. **Decide with both.** List a board when its node exists and either the probe allowed its major or the node was in the start-up list. Otherwise print the existing hint, and name 188 for ttyUSB rather than 166.

4. **Fix the comment.** Correct lines 77-79 to say that mknod is allowed for every device under Docker and only open() is checked.

5. **Skip discovery in the demo (optional).** When ESP32C5_DEMO is set and KISMET_SOURCES is empty, skip auto-discovery. The compose demo service has no cgroup rules, so otherwise it prints one hint per host board.

6. **Dockerfile header.** Add a separate docker run example for the kismet image that includes `--device-cgroup-rule 'c 166:* rmw' --device-cgroup-rule 'c 188:* rmw' --cap-add NET_ADMIN`. Leave the demo example without the rules.
verdicts:
I could not refute this finding. I checked it against the current files and in throwaway containers.

**The code.** In docker/entrypoint.sh, the comment at lines 77-79 says the node is made only where the device cgroup allows it, because mknod needs the same permission as open. The code at line 80 relies on that: `if [ -c "/dev/$tty" ]`. It is not true under Docker's defaults.

**Experiment on Docker Desktop 29.8** (debian:trixie-slim; containers named verify-*, run with --rm and gone afterwards). CapEff was a80425fb, which includes CAP_MKNOD.
- **No cgroup rule:** `mknod -m 660 /dev/ttyACM0 c 166 0` succeeds, as do 188:0 and 4:73, and `[ -c ]` is true. Opening the node gives "Operation not permitted".
- **With `--device-cgroup-rule 'c 166:* rmw'`:** opening 166:0 gives "No such device or address", which means the cgroup allowed it. 188 still gets EPERM.

This comes from runc, which always adds "allow mknod for any device" (`c *:* m`, `b *:* m`). Docker 26.1.5 on the Pi also runs containers with runc, so the Pi and the Linux PC should behave the same way. I did not test on the Pi, as instructed.

title: ESP32C5_WAIT stops waiting at the first board, so a hub of boards plugged in during the wait starts Kismet with only some of them
description: The start-up wait loop checks every 2 s and ends as soon as sources() returns anything. Boards on a hub enumerate one after another, a few hundred ms apart. A check that lands in the middle of that sees only the boards that have appeared so far. defs is then fixed for Kismet's whole life, and the boards that come later get device nodes but no source. Nothing says so: the "no ESP32-C5 board found" message prints only when n is 0.
failure_scenario: The kismet service starts on the Pi while the powered hub with the four boards is off, and logs "waiting up to 30 s". The user powers the hub, and ttyACM0..3 appear over about a second. The 2 s check sees ttyACM0 and ttyACM1 and leaves the loop. Kismet runs with 2 of the 4 boards until the container is restarted, and no log line mentions the other two.
evidence: entrypoint.sh:183-188 `while [ -z "$defs" ] && [ "$waited" -lt "${ESP32C5_WAIT:-30}" ]; do sleep 2; waited=$((waited + 2)); sync_devices; defs=$(sources 2>/dev/null); done`, then line 190 `for def in $defs` is used once.
suggested_fix: When the first board appears, keep checking until two checks in a row, about 2 s apart, return the same list, then start Kismet. Also log the number of boards used, so a short list is noticed.
fix:
The suggested fix is correct; here is a concrete, bounded version. Add it inside the existing `if`, after the first while loop at entrypoint.sh:183-188:

    # boards on a hub come up one after another: wait until the list stops changing
    prev=
    while [ -n "$defs" ] && [ "$defs" != "$prev" ] && [ "$waited" -lt $(( ${ESP32C5_WAIT:-30} + 10 )) ]; do
        prev=$defs
        sleep 2
        waited=$((waited + 2))
        sync_devices
        defs=$(sources 2>/dev/null)
    done

KISMET_SOURCES is unaffected: sources() returns it right away, so this block is never reached. Optionally, after the `for def` loop, log the total, e.g. `log "$n source(s)"`, so a short list stands out. The existing `source:` lines already name each board used.
verdicts:
I traced this in docker/entrypoint.sh and could not refute it. The wait loop only runs when the first `defs=$(sources)` (line 178) is empty and there is no demo board. Its condition at line 183, `while [ -z "$defs" ] && ...`, ends it on the first check that finds anything. Right before each check, sync_devices (line 186) makes a /dev node for every tty that is in sysfs at that moment. So find_boards returns exactly the boards that have enumerated so far. `defs` is then used once, at lines 190-194, and `exec kismet` follows. Nothing reads the list again, and the 1 s background sync loop only makes device nodes, not sources. compose.yaml does not set ESP32C5_WAIT, so the 30 s default applies, and it runs `restart: unless-stopped`. The only warning is at line 195, and it prints only when n is 0. The log does print a `source:` line for each board it used, so the user can see which boards were picked up, but nothing mentions the missing ones.

The failure is reachable in practice. Linux enumerates the ports of one hub one after another in hub_wq: a debounce of at least 100 ms, then reset, address and descriptors, then the cdc_acm probe. Four boards therefore take roughly 0.5-1.5 s to appear. A check every 2 s, at a random point in that window, lands in the middle a large share of the time. Plugging boards in one by one during the wait is even more likely to hit it.

title: The exec role ("anything else") makes no device nodes, so any command that opens a board fails with ENOENT
description: Only run_kismet and run_helper call keep_devices_in_sync. The documented third role (header line 8: run as a command, e.g. "kismet_cap_esp32c5 --list" or "sh") goes straight to `exec "$@"`. The container's /dev tmpfs then has no ttyACM nodes, while sysfs, and so --list, shows the boards.
failure_scenario: `sudo docker compose run --rm kismet kismet_cap_esp32c5 --list` shows esp32c5-ttyACM0. The user then runs `sudo docker compose run --rm kismet kismet_cap_esp32c5 --connect host:2501 --source esp32c5-ttyACM0`, or opens a shell and tries the port. The result is "cannot open /dev/ttyACM0: No such file or directory" for a board the same container just listed.
evidence: entrypoint.sh:263-265 `*) exec "$@" ;;` with no sync_devices. Only lines 164 and 229 call keep_devices_in_sync. The experiments here showed that a container's /dev starts with no ttyACM nodes (mknod was needed).
suggested_fix: Run `sync_devices` once (or keep_devices_in_sync, if the command is long-lived) before `exec "$@"`. It is cheap and harmless when there are no boards.

In docker/entrypoint.sh, change the last case branch to:

        exec "$@"

A plain `sync_devices` also fixes the reported failure (`--list` followed by `--connect`, or a shell). `keep_devices_in_sync` also keeps a long-lived exec'd `kismet_cap_esp32c5 --connect` working when a board comes back as another ttyACM number. Its 1-second loop ends with the container, and it is harmless when there are no boards or no cgroup rules, because the mknod failures are ignored.

I could not refute this finding. I traced it through the current files and ran one small experiment.

title: Setting only KISMET_PASSWORD (or only KISMET_USER) is ignored without a word once a login is kept in the volume
description: The warning "KISMET_USER and KISMET_PASSWORD go together; ignoring the one that is set" is only in the else branch, which runs when no login is kept. From the second start on, the elif branch (a login is in /root/.kismet) returns before it. So a half-set pair is dropped silently, and the user is left with the old, often generated, login and no hint why their password does not work.
failure_scenario: On the first start the entrypoint generated admin/e02d.... The user wants their own password and puts only KISMET_PASSWORD=mypass in .env, expecting the user to stay admin, then runs `docker compose up -d`. Kismet still has the generated password, logging in with mypass fails, and the log has nothing about it.
evidence: Experiment with one volume, a stand-in kismet and the real entrypoint. Run 1 (nothing set) logged "no web login was set, so Kismet's is now: user admin, password e02d3431c8794b16e3a0a1aa". Run 3 with `-e KISMET_PASSWORD=newpass` printed no warning, and the login file was unchanged: "httpd_username=admin httpd_password=e02d3431c8794b16e3a0a1aa". Code lines 113-120.
suggested_fix: Log the "go together" warning before the if chain whenever exactly one of the two is non-empty, whichever branch then runs. Or: when only KISMET_PASSWORD is set and a login is kept, keep that username and write the new password.

1. Line 113: both KISMET_USER and KISMET_PASSWORD are set.
2. Line 116: a login is kept in the volume. This branch does `return 0`.
3. The else branch. The warning "KISMET_USER and KISMET_PASSWORD go together; ignoring the one that is set" (lines 119-120) exists only here.

- Run 1, nothing set: printed the generated login, admin/06088e156a74507db79d83d4.

title: No /dev/serial/by-id in the container, so a board cannot be named stably in KISMET_SOURCES
description: The container no longer sees the host's /dev and runs no udev, and sync_devices makes only /dev/ttyACMn and /dev/ttyUSBn. The C helper explicitly supports device=/dev/serial/by-id/... links (capture_esp32c5.c:454, 1119, 1422), and they were available through the old /dev bind. Sources can now only be named by tty number, and that number can change between boots or after a hub power cycle. It also matters with another Espressif 303a:1001 device plugged in, where the entrypoint says to list sources explicitly.
failure_scenario: The user pins radios to boards with KISMET_SOURCES="esp32c5:device=/dev/serial/by-id/usb-Espressif_USB_JTAG_serial_debug_unit_<MAC>-if00,mode=zigbee ...", as works on the host. In the container every such source fails with "cannot open ...: No such file or directory". If they use esp32c5-ttyACM2 instead, a renumbering after a reboot can put the zigbee source on another board, or on an ESP32-C6 dev board that is also 303a:1001.
evidence: entrypoint.sh:42-62: sync_devices only makes "/dev/$tty" for ttyACM*/ttyUSB*. There is no by-id handling anywhere in docker/. capture_esp32c5.c:454 "The board's MAC from sysfs, following /dev/serial/by-id links to the tty".
suggested_fix: In sync_devices, also keep udev-style links /dev/serial/by-id/usb-<manufacturer>_<product>_<serial>-if<NN> -> ../../ttyACMn. Build them from the parent USB device's sysfs manufacturer, product and serial (spaces as '_') and the interface's bInterfaceNumber, and remove the links for ttys that are gone.
fix:
In entrypoint.sh, have sync_devices also keep udev-compatible links, created only while the tty node exists, and remove stale ones. Sketch (POSIX sh, add at the end of sync_devices):

    udev_enc() {  # udev usb_id encoding: trim, whitespace runs -> '_', other unsafe chars -> '_'
        printf '%s' "$1" | sed -e 's/^[[:space:]]*//' -e 's/[[:space:]]*$//' \
            -e 's/[[:space:]][[:space:]]*/_/g' -e 's/[^0-9A-Za-z#+.:=@_-]/_/g'
    }
    mkdir -p /dev/serial/by-id
    for dev in /sys/class/tty/ttyACM* /sys/class/tty/ttyUSB*; do
        [ -c "/dev/${dev##*/}" ] && [ -e "$dev/device" ] || continue
        tty=${dev##*/}
        case $tty in
            ttyACM*) intf=$(readlink -f "$dev/device"); port= ;;
            ttyUSB*) intf=$(readlink -f "$dev/device/.."); port=-port$(cat "$dev/device/port_number" 2>/dev/null || echo 0) ;;
        esac
        usb=$(readlink -f "$intf/..")
        [ -r "$usb/idVendor" ] && [ -r "$intf/bInterfaceNumber" ] || continue
        vendor=$(cat "$usb/manufacturer" 2>/dev/null) || vendor=$(cat "$usb/idVendor")
        model=$(cat "$usb/product" 2>/dev/null) || model=$(cat "$usb/idProduct")
        serial=$(cat "$usb/serial" 2>/dev/null) || serial=
        id="$(udev_enc "$vendor")_$(udev_enc "$model")${serial:+_$(udev_enc "$serial")}"
        link="/dev/serial/by-id/usb-$id-if$(cat "$intf/bInterfaceNumber")$port"
        [ "$(readlink "$link" 2>/dev/null)" = "../../$tty" ] || ln -sfn "../../$tty" "$link"
    done
    for link in /dev/serial/by-id/*; do   # drop links whose tty is gone
        [ -L "$link" ] || continue
        [ -c "$link" ] || rm -f "$link"
    done

Also give a by-id example next to the KISMET_SOURCES examples in the entrypoint header and compose.yaml, recommending by-id when other 303a:1001 devices are plugged in. The helper's `realpath` then resolves the link to `/dev/ttyACMn` inside the container, so `board_mac`, `flock` and `capif` all work unchanged. A longer-term alternative, outside this review because the C helper must not be edited, is a `mac=` source key in the helper.

The MAC check in `reopen_port` (lines 1121-1140) only protects a source after i

title: NET_ADMIN is granted to the whole Kismet container, which runs as root, only so the helper's capability drop does not crash
description: The kismet and helper services (through x-serial) and the demo service (line 74) add CAP_NET_ADMIN. The image has no USER, so the entrypoint and `exec kismet` run as root with Docker's default capabilities plus NET_ADMIN. The Kismet server is the process exposed to the network: it listens on 2501 on every interface, and it parses frames that anyone in radio range can send, on 802.11, BTLE and 802.15.4. None of the three radios needs NET_ADMIN, because the boards are serial ports. The capability is there only because kismet_cap_esp32c5 calls Kismet's cf_drop_most_caps() (capture_esp32c5.c:1590). That function puts CAP_NET_ADMIN and CAP_NET_RAW into the permitted set, and without NET_ADMIN in the bounding set that call fails and the helper crashes. The compose comment defends the choice with "It only reaches this container's own network". That understates the risk: CAP_NET_ADMIN over the container's netns is exactly the precondition for the nf_tables class of kernel privilege escalations. Docker's default seccomp profile blocks unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER) for this very reason, so that containers cannot obtain the capability, and adding it directly reopens that path. Everything else checked in this area is fine. The container is not on the host network. The device cgroup limits opens to majors 166 and 188. sysfs is read-only. Legacy port 3501 stays on the container's loopback, and kismet.conf at cfe427074 confirms `remote_capture_listen=127.0.0.1` is the default.
failure_scenario: A memory-safety bug in one of Kismet's dissectors (fed by radio frames from anyone nearby) or in its HTTP/websocket server on 2501 gives code execution as root with CAP_NET_ADMIN. From there, an nf_tables bug like CVE-2024-1086, CVE-2023-32233 or CVE-2022-1015 (the Pi's kernel lags on patches) is reachable through netlink, which the default seccomp profile allows. That turns container root into host root on the Raspberry Pi. Without NET_ADMIN these kernel paths are closed. The attacker would stay root in a container that can open only USB-serial devices.
evidence: compose.yaml:40-43: "# Kismet's capture helpers, run as root, keep NET_ADMIN and NET_RAW and drop every other ... (SIGSEGV) before it opens the board. It only reaches this container's own network.\n  cap_add: [NET_ADMIN]"; compose.yaml:74 `cap_add: [NET_ADMIN]  # for the capture helper, as above`; Dockerfile has no USER and entrypoint.sh:200 `exec kismet --no-ncurses "$@"`. capture_esp32c5.c:1588-1590: `cf_handler_remote_capture(caph); cf_jail_filesystem(caph); cf_drop_most_caps(caph);`. Kismet capture_framework.c:4938-4950: `cap_value_t cap_list[2] = { CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_NET_RAW }; ... cap_set_flag(caps, CAP_PERMITTED, ...); if (cap_set_proc(caps)) { ... cf_send_warning(...)`. Experiment: running the entrypoint's has_net_admin in a debian:trixie-slim container with --cap-add NET_ADMIN printed `has-net-admin`, `CapEff: 00000000a80435fb` (bit 12, CAP_NET_ADMIN, is set for every process in the container, not only the helper).
suggested_fix: Make the helper stop needing the capability. In capture_esp32c5.c, which this repo owns, replace `cf_drop_most_caps(caph);` with a drop that does not insist on NET_ADMIN, e.g. `if (prctl(PR_CAPBSET_READ, CAP_NET_ADMIN, 0, 0, 0) == 1) cf_drop_most_caps(caph); else { cap_t c = cap_init(); cap_set_proc(c); cap_free(c); }`. This helper needs no capability at all: it opens root-owned 0660 tty nodes as uid 0. Then remove `cap_add: [NET_ADMIN]` from x-serial and from demo, CAPS in tests/docker_smoke.sh, the NET_ADMIN advice in the Dockerfile header, and check_caps. Optionally mask Kismet's other bundled helpers (`mask_datasource_type=` in kismet_site.conf), because they would crash the same way on --list. Further hardening, to test on the Pi first: `cap_drop: [ALL]` plus `cap_add: [MKNOD]` (the entrypoint's mknod is the only privileged operation left), and `security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]`.
verdicts:
I could not refute any factual claim; each one checked out in the current files or in a small experiment.

What the files show:
- compose.yaml:43 puts `cap_add: [NET_ADMIN]` on x-serial, which the kismet and helper services inherit. compose.yaml:74 adds it to demo.
- The Dockerfile has no USER. Its header (lines 17-19) tells docker run users to add NET_ADMIN.
- entrypoint.sh:200 runs `exec kismet` as root, after check_caps (lines 134-154) warns when NET_ADMIN is missing.
- capture_esp32c5.c:1588-1590 calls `cf_handler_remote_capture; cf_jail_filesystem; cf_drop_most_caps`.
- In Kismet cfe4270, capture_framework.c:4925-4978 sets NET_ADMIN and NET_RAW in the permitted and inheritable sets. When cap_set_proc fails, it calls cf_send_warning, which is cf_send_message and then cf_prepare_packet, before the IPC channel exists.
- The helper needs no capability at all. Its only privileged-looking operations are open O_RDWR, flock, termios and TIOCMBIC on nodes the entrypoint creates as root with mode 0660 (entrypoint.sh:55), plus reads of world-readable sysfs.
- Nothing else in the image needs NET_ADMIN: the boards are serial, the network is a bridge, and 2501 is an unprivileged port.

1. alpine with default capabilities: `nft add table inet probe` fails with "Operation not permitted", CapEff a80425fb. With `--cap-add NET_ADMIN` the table is created and CapEff is a80435fb. So Docker's default seccomp profile does not block nf_tabl

title: mknod is always allowed, so the board check never notices a missing device_cgroup_rule; the demo and plain docker run add boards they cannot open
description: find_boards takes the presence of /dev/<tty> as proof that the device cgroup allows the board. The comment above it says so: "The node is made only where the device cgroup allows it (mknod needs the same permission as open)". That is not how Docker works. Its default device rules grant 'm' (mknod) on every character and block device, and only 'rw' is limited to the allowed majors. So sync_devices always creates /dev/ttyACM*, the `[ -c ]` test is always true, and the else branch with its hint is dead code. This matters wherever the rules are missing. One case is the compose demo service, which has no device_cgroup_rules. Another is a plain `docker run` of the Kismet image following the Dockerfile header, which mentions only --cap-add NET_ADMIN. The real boards then become Kismet sources that fail on open with EPERM. This only makes the rules less visible to the user. It does not widen host access, because the open is still denied.
failure_scenario: On the Pi, with ESP32-C5 boards plugged in, the user runs `docker compose --profile demo up demo`, or `docker run --cap-add NET_ADMIN ... esp32c5-kismet` without --device-cgroup-rule. The entrypoint logs `source: esp32c5-ttyACM0:mode=wifi` for every board and passes them to Kismet. Each one fails with "cannot open /dev/ttyACM0: Operation not permitted" and Kismet keeps retrying. The hint telling the user to add `--device-cgroup-rule 'c 166:* rmw'` is never printed. In the demo, the error sources sit next to the fake board.
evidence: entrypoint.sh:77-85: `# The node is made only where the device cgroup allows it (mknod needs the same permission as open), so its absence is the answer. ... if [ -c "/dev/$tty" ]; then echo "$tty" else log "found $tty in sysfs but the container may not use it...`. compose.yaml:66-81: the demo service has no `<<: *serial`. Experiment on Docker Desktop 29.8.0 with debian:trixie-slim. Without rules: `mknod ok: crw-rw---- 1 root root 166, 9 ... /dev/ttyACM9`, `[ -c ] true`, then open: `cannot create /dev/ttyACM9: Operation not permitted`. With `--device-cgroup-rule 'c 166:* rmw'`: open gives `No such device or address` (allowed, no device). `mknod /dev/sdz b 8 0` also succeeds without rules.
suggested_fix: Probe each major on a minor that no device uses, so no real port is opened and DTR/RTS do not move. EPERM means the cgroup denies it, ENXIO means it allows it. The following worked under dash in both cases (no rules: `166 denied 188 denied`; with only c 166: `166 allowed 188 denied`): `may_open_major() { m=255; while [ -e "/sys/dev/char/$1:$m" ]; do m=$((m-1)); done; probe=/dev/.esp32c5-probe-$1; rm -f "$probe"; mknod "$probe" c "$1" "$m" 2>/dev/null || return 1; err=$( { : < "$probe"; } 2>&1 ); rm -f "$probe"; case "$err" in *"not permitted"*) return 1;; esac; }`. Use it in find_boards instead of `[ -c ]`, so the hint fires, and have sync_devices skip denied majors. Also correct the comment.
fix:
The suggested fix is essentially right. Refine it as follows.

**1. Add the probe to entrypoint.sh.** It never opens a real port, so DTR/RTS do not move:
```sh
may_open_major() {  # may_open_major MAJOR: does the device cgroup allow read/write on it?
    m=255; while [ "$m" -gt 0 ] && [ -e "/sys/dev/char/$1:$m" ]; do m=$((m-1)); done
    probe=/dev/.esp32c5-probe-$1; rm -f "$probe"
    mknod "$probe" c "$1" "$m" 2>/dev/null || return 1
    err=$( { : < "$probe"; } 2>&1 ); rm -f "$probe"
    case "$err" in *"not permitted"*) return 1 ;; esac   # EPERM = cgroup; ENXIO/ENODEV = allowed
}
```
LC_ALL is unset in the image, so strerror is in English.

**2. Use it in find_boards.** Replace `if [ -c "/dev/$tty" ]` with `major=$(cut -d: -f1 "$dev/dev"); if [ -c "/dev/$tty" ] && may_open_major "$major"; then`. Probe each major once and cache the result.

**3. Optionally, skip denied majors in sync_devices,** so that no unusable nodes appear.

**4. Rewrite the comment at :77-79.** Docker (runc) allows mknod of any device, so the node existing proves nothing. Only an open shows the cgroup rule, and it is done on an unused minor so no board's reset lines move.

**5. Also consider the demo.** With the probe, the demo on a machine with boards would print the device_cgroup_rules hint instead of adding failing sources. Cleaner still: skip board auto-detection when ESP32C5_DEMO is set and KISMET_SOURCES is empty, since the demo is meant to need no hardware.

**6. Mention the rule for plain `docker run`.** The Dockerfile header's docker run example should show `--device-cgroup-rule 'c 166:* rmw'` for real boards, or say it is only for the demo.
verdicts:
I could not refute this finding. I confirmed it from the files and with throwaway containers on Docker Desktop 29.8.0 (cgroup2, debian:trixie-slim).

**Code path.** Both roles reach the board check the same way:
- `run_kismet` (entrypoint.sh:164) and `run_helper` (:229) call `keep_devices_in_sync` before `sources()`/`find_boards`.
- The `ESP32C5_WAIT` loop also calls `sync_devices` before `sources`.
- `sync_devices` runs `mknod -m 660 /dev/ttyACMn c 166 n` for every tty in sysfs. A container sees the host's `/sys/class/tty`, including `idVendor`/`idProduct`.
- `find_boards` (:80) then only tests `[ -c /dev/$tty ]`.

**Why the check is always true.** runc's specconv `AllowedDevices` adds 'm' for every char and block device (`c *:* m`, `b *:* m`) on top of the rules the user sets. Docker keeps CAP_MKNOD by default, so mknod always succeeds. The `else` branch with the `--device-cgroup-rule` hint only runs if mknod itself fails (cap-drop MKNOD, rootless, userns). In the default case it is dead code, and the comment at :77-79 ("mknod needs the same permission as open") is wrong.

**Experiment:**

| Container | mknod 166:9 | `[ -c ]` | open |
|---|---|---|---|
| No rules | ok | true | "Operation not permitted" |
| `--cap-add NET_ADMIN` only (the demo's settings) | ok | true | EPERM |
| `--device-cgroup-rule 'c 166:* rmw'` | ok | true | "No such device or address" (allowed, no device) |

**Where it happens:**
- The compose `demo` service has no `<<: *serial`.
- The Dockerfile header

title: CI: `:demo` moves on any v tag without '-', but `:latest` only on valid semver, so a tag like v1.3 splits the two images
description: The Kismet image gets `latest` from metadata-action's latest=auto. That applies only when type=semver matches a valid, non-pre-release version. The demo's floating tag instead uses its own test: `startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v') && !contains(github.ref_name, '-')`. The trigger `tags: ["v*"]` also accepts tags that are not semver: v1.3, v2, vtest, v1.2.3.4. For those, metadata-action skips every semver rule with a warning, so the Kismet image gets only `sha-xxxxxxx`: no version tag and no latest. The demo image is still tagged `:demo`. The pins, permissions, lower-casing, cache scopes, digest merge and pre-release handling are otherwise right. All seven action SHAs match their tags upstream (checked with git ls-remote). Pre-releases like v1.1.0-rc.1 get neither latest nor demo, and {{major}}.{{minor}} is skipped for them.
failure_scenario: The maintainer pushes `v1.3` (two parts) as a release. The publish job tags the Kismet image only as `sha-abc1234`, so `:latest` stays on the previous release and there is no `:1.3`. The demo image is tagged `:demo`. `docker pull ...:demo` and `...:latest` now give different releases, and compose.yaml's kismet and helper services keep the old `:latest` although a release was made.
evidence: docker.yml:19 `tags: ["v*"]`; :178 `flavor: latest=auto`; :180-181 `type=semver,pattern={{version}}` / `{{major}}.{{minor}}`; :196 `type=raw,value=demo,suffix=,enable=${{ startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v') && !contains(github.ref_name, '-') }}`. metadata-action@c299e40 src/meta.ts procSemver: `if (!semver.valid(vraw)) { core.warning(...not a valid semver...); return version; }`. Experiment with node-semver 7: `v1.3 valid= null ... demo-enable(no dash)= true`, `v2 valid= null ... true`, `vtest valid= null ... true`, `v1.2.3-rc.1 valid= 1.2.3-rc.1 prerelease= [ 'rc', 1 ] ... false`.
suggested_fix: Tie the demo's floating tag to the decision made for the Kismet image: `type=raw,value=demo,suffix=,enable=${{ contains(steps.meta.outputs.tags, format('{0}:latest', env.REGISTRY_IMAGE)) }}`. Also, or instead, narrow the trigger to semver tags: `tags: ["v[0-9]+.[0-9]+.[0-9]+*"]`.
fix:
Primary fix. On docker.yml line 196, give the demo its floating tag only when the Kismet image got `:latest`. Checking membership in the JSON array is stricter than a substring match on the newline-joined `tags` output:

    type=raw,value=demo,suffix=,enable=${{ contains(fromJSON(steps.meta.outputs.json).tags, format('{0}:latest', env.REGISTRY_IMAGE)) }}

The suggested `contains(steps.meta.outputs.tags, format('{0}:latest', env.REGISTRY_IMAGE))` also works, because no other tag starts with `:latest`.

Optional, on top of the primary fix and not instead of it: stop non-semver tags from triggering the workflow at all. List two patterns so that a trailing `*` does not admit `v1.2.3.4`:

    tags: ["v[0-9]+.[0-9]+.[0-9]+", "v[0-9]+.[0-9]+.[0-9]+-*"]

If you narrow the trigger, keep the line 196 change anyway, so that `v1.2.3+build-1` gets both `:latest` and `:demo`.
verdicts:
I confirmed this against the current docker.yml and against metadata-action at the pinned SHA c299e40 (v5.10.0; the local clone is in scratchpad/dockrev/metadata-action/src/meta.ts).

1. **The trigger lets non-semver tags through.** docker.yml:19 has `tags: ["v*"]`. GitHub does not apply path filters to tag pushes, so any tag starting with `v` runs the workflow. The `publish` job's `if` (line 148) and `PUSH` (line 42) test only `startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v')`, so such a tag is also published.

2. **The Kismet image gets no version tag and no `:latest`.** Its metadata step (lines 173-183) uses `latest=auto`. In meta.ts `procSemver`, `if (!semver.valid(vraw)) { core.warning(...); return version; }` runs before `latest = true` is ever set. `procRefBranch` does nothing on a tag ref, so the only tag left comes from `procSha`. `procSha` calls `setVersion(..., latest=auto ? false : ...)`, so `version.latest` ends up false. I checked with node-semver 7 in scratchpad/semver: `v1.3`, `v2`, `vtest` and `v1.2.3.4` all give `valid=null`. For those tags the Kismet image is tagged only `sha-xxxxxxx`.

3. **The demo image still gets `:demo`.** Its rule on line 196 enables `type=raw,value=demo,suffix=` whenever the ref starts with `refs/tags/v` and the name has no `-`. That expression is true for all four of those tags, and `procRaw` has no semver check.

4. **The job does not fail.** The Inspect step works on `sha-...` and `demo`. The two floating tags silently point at different rel

title: CI comment says arm64 runners need paid larger runners in a private repo; they have been standard since January 2026
description: The header says the ubuntu-24.04-arm runner "is free for public repositories; a private one needs larger runners, or the arm64 row removed from the matrix". Since 2026-01-29, GitHub's standard arm64 runners (ubuntu-24.04-arm, ubuntu-22.04-arm) also work in private repositories and count against the plan's free minutes. They have 2 vCPUs there instead of 4. The workflow runs unchanged in a private repo. The advice to drop the arm64 row would remove the image for the main deployment, the Raspberry Pi. The Dockerfile's JOBS calculation already adapts to 2 cores. Only the headroom under `timeout-minutes: 120` for a cold-cache Kismet build is smaller. I did not measure it.
failure_scenario: The repository is made private (it has no remote yet). Following the comment, the maintainer deletes the linux/arm64 matrix row. Releases then publish amd64-only manifests. On the Pi, `docker compose up` cannot use ghcr.io/...:latest (no linux/arm64 entry) and builds Kismet locally, which takes an hour or more.
evidence: docker.yml:7-9: "Each architecture builds on its own native runner ... The arm64 runner (ubuntu-24.04-arm) is free for public repositories; a private one needs larger runners, or the arm64 row removed from the matrix." GitHub changelog 2026-01-29, "arm64 standard runners are now available in private repositories": ubuntu-24.04-arm is supported in private repositories with two vCPUs and counts toward the plan's free minutes.
suggested_fix: Correct the comment. The arm64 row works in private repositories too, on 2 vCPUs and counting toward the plan's minutes. If a cold build approaches the limit there, raise timeout-minutes for the arm64 row rather than removing the row.
fix: Replace lines 8-9 with wording along these lines: "The arm64 runner (ubuntu-24.04-arm) is free in public repositories. Since 2026-01-29 it also runs in private repositories, on fewer cores, and uses the plan's included minutes." Do not state a vCPU count, because GitHub's pages disagree. Do not suggest removing the arm64 row, because the Raspberry Pi uses that image. If a cold build on a private repository's arm64 runner gets close to the limit, give the arm64 row more time. `timeout-minutes` is set per job, so add a `timeout: 180` value to that matrix row (and `timeout: 120` to the amd64 row). Then set `timeout-minutes: ${{ matrix.timeout }}`.
verdicts:
I could not refute this finding. Lines 7-9 of .github/workflows/docker.yml say: "The arm64 runner (ubuntu-24.04-arm) is free for public repositories; a private one needs larger runners, or the arm64 row removed from the matrix." The matrix at lines 52-53 does use `runner: ubuntu-24.04-arm` for linux/arm64.

GitHub's changelog of 2026-01-29, "arm64 standard runners are now available in private repositories" (github.blog/changelog/2026-01-29-arm64-standard-runners-are-now-available-in-private-repositories/), says Linux and Windows arm64 standard runners are now supported in all repositories. It lists the labels ubuntu-24.04-arm, ubuntu-22.04-arm and windows-11-arm. In private repositories the runners have 2 vCPUs, and usage counts toward the plan's included free minutes. GitHub's hosted-runner reference page (docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/runners/github-hosted-runners) also lists ubuntu-24.04-arm for private repositories. Public jobs are free; private jobs use the plan's included minutes and are then billed.

So the comment is out of date. A private repository does not need larger runners, and the workflow runs there unchanged. The comment's other suggestion, removing the arm64 row, would drop the linux/arm64 image. That image is the one the Raspberry Pi deployment uses. The Dockerfile's JOBS calculation (line 60) is based on nproc and MemAvailable, so it already adapts to a smaller runner.

Two small points about the evidence. First, the reference page may now list 2 CP
